I am 79 years old. I have farmed this land in Quzhou since I was nine years old. My father taught me, and I learned the rest by watching and doing. I never went past primary school, but I know every piece of this 4.1 mu like the back of my hand.

For my winter wheat, I do what I did last year. Last year I got about 430 jin per mu, and that is good enough for us. I plant Jimai 22 — the same improved variety I have used for many years, the one Lao Zhang across the road also plants. In October, before sowing, I spread one full bag of compound fertilizer on each mu — that is 50 kg, the 15-15-15 kind — and then I run the rotary tiller to mix it in. I do not skip this. At green-up time in March, I top-dress with half a bag of urea per mu, about 25 kg. Fertilizer is expensive now, maybe 90 or 100 yuan a bag, but if I use less, the wheat turns yellow and I lose more than I save. A bad harvest is a disaster; wasting a little fertilizer is just money. I irrigate three times from my well: once before winter so the wheat does not freeze, once at jointing when the stems start growing, and once when the heads come out. For pests, I spray twice — once in spring for aphids, and once before flowering for the rust. My wife and I do this ourselves. Hired labor is 150 yuan a day now, too much for us.

For the summer maize, I plant right after I cut the wheat in early June. I use Zhengdan 958, a hybrid maize — everyone around here uses it, and it gives solid ears. Before planting, I put down 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu and till it in with the rotary machine. When the maize gets to knee-height, I spread another 25 kg of urea per mu. I irrigate twice: once after planting if the ground is dry, and once when the tassels come out. Two pesticide sprays — one for corn borer, and one more later if the armyworms show up. I expect about 460 jin per mu if the weather holds.

I do not try new things anymore. My neighbor tried some fancy new fertilizer two years ago and his crop grew strange. I will stick to what I know. My wife and I are old, so we keep it simple and do what worked before. Better to spend a bit more on fertilizer than to risk a bad year. We need the grain.
